title: TypeScript Type Assertions & Safe Narrowing: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on `as` assertions, the non-null `!`, `as const`, `satisfies`, `unknown` vs `any`, and when to use type guards instead of assertions.

chapters.title: Assertions vs Types: The Mental Model
points: An assertion (`x as T`) tells the compiler 'trust me' — it changes the static type only, emits no runtime code, and does no conversion or check
`as` only allows casts where one type is assignable to the other (sufficiently overlapping); `'a' as number` errors, but `x as unknown as number` forces it
Annotation (`const a: T = v`) checks v against T; assertion (`v as T`) overrides the checker — a wrong assertion becomes a runtime crash, not a compile error
Safe assertions: narrowing a wider type to a known subtype (`document.getElementById('a') as HTMLInputElement`); also upcasting is always safe
Angle-bracket form `<T>x` is equivalent but is invalid in .tsx files, so use `as`

chapters.title: Unsafe Assertions and the Non-Null Operator
points: Asserting an object literal `{} as User` silences missing-property errors, so `user.name.length` throws at runtime; prefer a typed annotation or `Partial<User>`
Double assertion `x as unknown as T` bypasses all overlap checks — a red flag, treat it as a last resort
Non-null `x!` removes `null | undefined` from the type at compile time only; at runtime `null!.foo` still throws a TypeError
Use `?.`, `??`, or an explicit `if (x)` check instead of `!`; reserve `!` for cases the compiler can't see, e.g. `map.get(k)!` right after `map.has(k)`
`JSON.parse(s) as User` and `fetch().json() as T` are unsafe: no validation occurs, so validate with a type guard or a schema library (zod)

chapters.title: as const and Literal Types
points: `let x = 'a'` widens to `string`; `const x = 'a'` keeps the literal type `'a'`; object properties widen even with const, so `{ mode: 'dark' }` has `mode: string`
`as const` freezes inference: literals stay narrow, objects become `readonly` recursively, and arrays become readonly tuples (`['a','b'] as const` is `readonly ['a','b']`)
Derive a union from a const array: `const ROLES = ['admin','user'] as const; type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number]` gives `'admin' | 'user'`
`as const` is compile-time only (does not call Object.freeze) and works only on literal expressions, not on variables or function calls
Passing a widened `string` to a param typed `'GET' | 'POST'` errors; fix it with `as const` on the value rather than asserting `as 'GET'`

chapters.title: satisfies vs Annotation vs as
points: `expr satisfies T` (TS 4.9+) checks the expression against T but keeps the expression's own narrower inferred type
Annotation `const c: Colors = {...}` widens to Colors and loses specifics; `satisfies Colors` keeps `red: [number, number, number]` and still errors on typos and missing keys
Comparison: annotation = checks and widens; `as` = no check and overrides; `satisfies` = checks and keeps narrow type
`satisfies` also catches excess properties in object literals, while `as` silently allows them
Combine them: `{ ... } as const satisfies Config` yields a readonly narrow value that is validated against Config

chapters.title: unknown vs any and Type Guards vs Assertions
points: `any` turns off checking: it is assignable to and from everything and allows any property access or call; it spreads silently through code
`unknown` is the safe top type: anything is assignable to it, but you must narrow it before use, and you can't access properties on it or call it
Narrow `unknown` with `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, or a custom guard `function isUser(x: unknown): x is User` — the guard's body is your responsibility; a wrong predicate lies to the compiler
Assertion functions `function assert(x: unknown): asserts x is User` throw on failure and narrow the code after the call; the guard returns a boolean, the assertion throws

Rule of thumb: type guard or validation for untrusted data (API, JSON, catch blocks with `useUnknownInCatchVariables`); assertion only when you hold knowledge the compiler can't see; `any` almost never

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Assertions, satisfies, unknown
points: `as T` = no runtime effect and no check, `x!` = strips null/undefined at compile time only, `as unknown as T` = last resort
`as const` = literal + readonly + tuple; `(typeof ARR)[number]` = union of the elements
`satisfies T` = validate without widening; annotation = validate and widen; `as` = override
`unknown` = must narrow first; `any` = unchecked and contagious; prefer `unknown` for untrusted input
Narrowing toolbox: `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, `x is T` guard, `asserts x is T`, schema validation (zod) for external data
